name: Scone
summary: The Moot Hill above the Tay where Scottish kings were made, from an assembly of 906 to the crowning of Robert the Bruce in 1306 — and the abbey Edward I stripped of its stone.
overview: Scone was one of medieval Scotland’s most important royal ceremonial sites. Kings were inaugurated there, and the place carried the memory of the Stone of Scone and the public rituals of Scottish kingship.
Robert the Bruce’s coronation at Scone in 1306 gave his contested seizure of power the form of traditional kingship, even though his political position remained fragile.
knownFor: The Moot Hill, where Scottish kings were inaugurated

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Scone mattered because medieval Scottish kingship was performed as well as inherited. Inauguration at Scone linked a ruler to the kingdom’s ceremonial past and to the political community that recognized him.

The site sits on the left bank of the Tay a little north of Perth, at the centre of the old Pictish and Alban heartland rather than at the centre of the later kingdom. Two things stood there: the low mound called the Moot Hill, where the ceremony happened in the open, and the abbey church beside it, where the ecclesiastical part of the rite was performed.

contentSections.title: Moot Hill
paragraphs: The earliest notice of assembly at Scone is from 906, when Constantine II and Bishop Cellach met on the hill and swore to keep the laws and customs of the church — a king and a bishop binding themselves in public, which is the shape every later ceremony there kept.

The mound is small and artificial-looking, and the tradition that it was raised from earth carried in the boots of men swearing fealty is a later story rather than evidence. What matters is its function: a raised place where a man was set in a seat, in the open, before the people who had chosen him.

contentSections.title: The abbey
paragraphs: Augustinian canons were brought from Nostell in Yorkshire and settled at Scone between about 1114 and 1122 under royal patronage, on a site that had already been a religious centre. In December 1164, in the reign of Malcolm IV, the priory was raised to the status of an abbey.

It became one of the wealthiest houses in Scotland, held relics of Saint Fergus that drew pilgrims, and served as a royal residence as well as a monastery. Its musical life lasted to the end: the composer Robert Carver, one of the finest of the late medieval north, worked there into the sixteenth century.

contentSections.title: Making a king at Scone
paragraphs: The rite had two halves, one in the abbey church and one on the hill, where the new king was seated on the Stone of Scone, presented to the assembly, and had his descent recited aloud by a royal poet. The inauguration of the seven-year-old heir in 1249 is the first for which both a written account and a picture survive, and it shows the form already fixed.

John Balliol was made king there in 1292 after the great cause that Edward I of England had arbitrated. Robert the Bruce was crowned at Scone on 25 March 1306, six weeks after killing John Comyn at Dumfries, in a hurried ceremony that borrowed the old forms precisely because his title needed them. Edward Balliol was crowned on the same ground on 24 September 1332.

contentSections.title: 1296 and after
paragraphs: The site was associated with royal assemblies, inauguration, and the Stone of Scone before Edward I removed the stone to England in 1296. Even after that removal, Scone retained symbolic force.

That is the point of the theft and the point of its failure. Taking the stone to Westminster was meant to end Scottish kingship as a thing that could be performed; three men were made king at Scone after it went, and the ceremony simply proceeded without it.

contentSections.title: The end of the abbey
paragraphs: A Protestant mob from Dundee burned the abbey in 1559, during the Scottish Reformation, and it was never rebuilt. The lands passed eventually to the Murray family, later Earls of Mansfield, whose house — Scone Palace — stands beside the hill today.
The abbey’s own footprint was lost until geophysical survey traced it in the ground, showing a church considerably larger than had been assumed. The Moot Hill survives, with a small chapel on it.
